This specific arrangement applies to certain followers of particular Vedic branches (*śākhins*), because [this is established] in the *smṛtis* of Manu and others, as well as in the *purāṇas* such as the *Matsya-purāṇa*.

Setting aside the primary *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] and the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* ritual, the instruction regarding the time for the offering of the *piṇḍas* occurs precisely before the meal; for this very reason, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* should explain that the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha takes place only after the meal. However, for those for whom the *piṇḍas* [are offered] in the *Gṛhya* [sūtras] and other texts—
The specific times for giving have been mentioned; however, among them, the most excellent is at the end of life— this alone is [the primary one].
15th Chapter: The Section on the Offering of Pindas in the Bākalpa.

It is proper to take [the portion] from the plate. Here, the alternatives regarding the time for giving the *piṇḍas* and so forth have been explained. Thus ends the section on the times for giving the *piṇḍas*.
Now, regarding the places for the offering of the *piṇḍas*:
first, having performed the offering of the *piṇḍas* near the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the procedure for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is followed;
and in [the rites] beginning with "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*), there is the application of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* as a model.

If fire is available in that place, one should offer the *piṇḍas* in its very vicinity. Likewise, Devala, while describing the offering of the *piṇḍas* at the time following the feeding of the Brahmins, has prescribed the placing of the *piṇḍas* upon the ground and their adornment with collyrium and other ornaments; immediately thereafter, he speaks of the *agnihotra*.
Having placed that offering for the *homa* into the receptacle where the previous *piṇḍas* were deposited,
the twice-born [priest] should subsequently cause the *vāmala* (cooked food) to be given to those *piṇḍas* near this fire.

Thus, having placed the piṇḍas in this manner as described, one should immediately after these piṇḍas offer cooked food (*pakvānna*) as an oblation (*naivedya*) to them. By stating that the fire-oblation (*agnihoma*) takes place in the vicinity of the piṇḍas, it is implied that the piṇḍas themselves are to be placed near the fire. However, in the absence of fire—

Regarding the statements of Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, and Yājñavalkya concerning the scattering [of the rice], Madhuśarman and others teach that "having scattered in three ways" means one should give the balls (piṇḍas) near the scattered [rice].
In that context, because there is no interval between the scattered [rice] and the nearby location, the offering of the balls is not performed upon the scattered [rice] itself.

Thus, having conceived the notion that [the recipient] is an Arhat because of such a statement, and intending to offer a ball of food (*piṇḍa*) to him, Vyāsa spoke this rule in order to restrain the donor from doing so:
"Having cleared a space the measure of a fathom (*vyāma*), one should cause the ball of food to be given."
"Wherein even the drops do not reach, nor are they found.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,
Chapter 5, Section on *Śrāddha*: "In that context," meaning in that performance of the *śrāddha*, [one should measure] a space of three *aratnis* from the place where the remnants are located.

Having abandoned [the previous spot], one should offer the *piṇḍas* at the place where one stands. A hand with the little finger raised is called "the fire" (*agni*). And this separation should be understood as applying to Brahmins who are highly skilled and well-behaved, provided that the area for offering the *piṇḍas* has not been reached by drops of water from the sipping of water (*ācamana*). [Regarding] the sipping of water—
But in the event of an attack by wild animals, one should leave even a greater distance.
Thus it is said: "Where, for those who are touching [the water]... and so forth; that is, for the Brahmins who are *upaspṛśatām*—that is, *ācāmatām* (sipping water).
In that place which the drops (vindavaḥ) do not reach, there the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍadāna) is performed.
Likewise, Pāraskara states that the abandonment [of food] should be greater than the measure of a chariot-track:
"The offering of the rice-ball is prescribed at a distance of one fathom (bāhumātra) from the Brahmins."
The meaning is that one must kill the Brahmins eating at the *śrāddha* from a distance of one fathom (*bāhumātra*) or further away.
Regarding the word "viprāṇām" (of the Brahmins), there is an alternative reading, "pātrāṇām" (of the vessels).

Even in that case, when there is a suspicion of water-drops reaching [the ground], one should explain the meaning of the statement regarding the disposal of food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa-nidhi*), while indicating the direction—

Regarding the instruction on the rules of restraint (*niyama*), Ātreya states that one should abandon a space measuring more than the length of an arm. Having invoked the ancestors, one should place three blades of grass before them;
the food remaining there is divided into three portions for the ancestors, and the vessel containing the remnants of the food for the ancestors is designated as the *paitrya* vessel.

This is an illustration [of the rule] for Brahmins as well, because the principle is the same regarding the intervention of their leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*). "From the place suitable for sitting" means from the portion of the ground fit for sitting; and that is restricted to the western part of that area, since it is there that the required interval is obtained. Otherwise, in a narrow space...

Otherwise, it would follow that there is no fixed interval [between the offerings]. And in that case, it might happen that the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is made even in the very spot where one has just eaten. Furthermore, it is impossible to conceive of a fixed acquisition [of merit] through a non-fixed arrangement.
Alternatively, the area over which the ancestors are honored while they eat constitutes the extent of the ancestors' seat (*āsana*).

Vessels are obtained by means of a limit (*avadhi*); for the ancestors are joined with that much space.
"In front" (*śrayataḥ*) means to the east; however, there is no restriction regarding the directions such as behind or the two sides.
Furthermore, regarding the apprehension that water droplets might fall [into the fire], Jātūkarṇya states that one should perform an even greater renunciation:

so that neither the water-sprinklers nor the droplets reach them."
The distance between the tips of the two outstretched arms is called a *vyāma*. However,

With the intention that the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) should be performed even when the distance is limited by the *śrāddha* marriage rites and so forth, for the sake of favoring those of varying status, it was stated:

"where [the water] touches those who sip," and so on. This refers only to the instruction regarding the mouthfuls being free from the falling of drops during sipping (*ācamana*), and not to the words concerning fire and the like.

The purpose is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthatva*). Regarding the *maṅkaṭa* [spot]: at the location of the *śrāddha*, one should specifically perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) so that no water splashes out; having ensured that the place is not defiled by being separated from the fire and other such elements by means of the *maṅkaṭa*, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*) there—such is the established rule (*vyavasthā*).
Regarding the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to be offered prior to the feeding of the Brahmins, Devala states concerning specific locations and other details:

In Kāyā, there is indeed Hastinī, in the presence of Vastadohitra.

The "elephant's shadow" (*hasticchāyā*) refers to that which is favored by the elephant during the offering of the funeral ball (*piṇḍadāna*). Since this specific region, when joined with the offering of alms (*piṇḍadāna*), will bring about the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), what is the point of insisting on the context? This is clearly stated in the section on "The Elephant's Shadow" (*gajacchāyā*);
therein is the mention of obtaining permission (*anujñā*).
Thus end the locations for the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*).
Now, the procedure for the offering of the rice-ball:
regarding that offering of the rice-ball, Devala states that one who desires to perform it must first take up a water-pot containing the remains of the deceased.
Then, taking a water-pot filled with water along with darbha grass and sitting down in front of them, he should announce the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas).
Thereafter, permitted by them, he should go toward the southern direction.

Having taken up the *piṇḍa*— which is like a ball of food, placed upon *darbha* grass, and accompanied by the *pavitra*— with water, and having grasped it firmly with both hands, one should sit before the Brāhmaṇas and perform the inquiry intended to request permission, saying, "I shall perform the offering of the *piṇḍas*. One should present the *piṇḍa* offerings to them. Then, having been authorized by the Brahmins with the words "Do so," one should go toward the southern direction. It should not be performed behind [the Brahmins], because it has already been expressed by the suffix *ciṇ*; furthermore, with respect to the Brahmins standing facing north, proceeding toward the southern direction would be improper. Nevertheless, it is for the sake of attaining excellence that [the action] is performed while facing south. (Note: Variant reading *kha* reads "for the sake of attaining excellence for one who is indeed facing south.")
In this discourse, the section concerning the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa).

In order to give meaning to the injunction "having stood [there], he goes toward the southern direction," it is understood that he has come two or three steps from his place of questioning; or else, "having sat down in front" means having sat down facing eastward.

One should pose the question. Then, having gone toward the southern direction and facing south, one should perform the offering of the *piṇḍas*. The water-pot (*kalaśa*) should be kept there for the purpose of procuring the water required for all the rites, such as sprinkling (*mārjana*), washing (*avanejana*), and so forth, which are necessary for the preparation of those *piṇḍas*. That collection belongs specifically to those for whom some ritual act is prescribed by means of the *kalaśa*. Śālaṅkāyana clarifies this point— that for some, this is a collection of the *kaṇṭhaka* verses— by stating that the mention of the *anu-jā* occurs even without a formal collection (*tat-saṃgraha*).
Having obtained permission for the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍāvāpa*), one should remain restrained in speech, body, and mind.
Then, with this [mantra], one should offer a handful of rice balls.

In a secluded and clean place, one should prepare a seat for oneself;

"Upasliptam" means smeared with cow dung and cow urine on the ground, according to the statement, "The earth is indeed the cow's dung. It has been stated that [the ground] must be pure; or, as it is naturally so, it may be "beautiful" (śubha). In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,

"Or it may be quadrangular. "Maṇḍala" means circular in shape; "caturasra" means four-cornered.

"Sloping toward the south" means inclined toward the south. "Large" refers to a plot of ground that is clearly visible and sufficient for the placement of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*); although its extent is already established by that [requirement], this is a restatement for the sake of clarity.

Alternatively, this is the procedure for [the rite] which possesses slightly greater extensiveness than the establishment of the offering of the *piṇḍas* due to its sufficient breadth. Indeed, a great rite must be performed through the mouth of the Pitṛs and Aryaman. And so it is stated in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa:

"Khaṇḍana" refers to breaking or splitting; "patha" refers to rubbing against the ground and so forth; "ucakhana-kriyā" refers to the act of scratching or making lines. At times, there is the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for the groups beginning with the father, mother, and maternal grandfather. He strives; indeed, for the sake of warding off harm, he offers prayers.

And this is optional, for according to the Vedic scripture, "the south is the direction of the ancestors," one may face the south.

Because [the direction] from the "tvā" [suffix] and so forth is understood, and because we observe both facing south (*dakṣiṇābhimukhatva*) and ending toward the south (*dakṣiṇāpavargatva*). "Hā pacana! To the south-east is the place for cooking.

He should touch [the water] while reciting: "O Fathers, come hither with the speed of thought.

"He places the firebrand at the far end with the mantra 'ye rūpāṇi'";

Then, he places a firebrand (ulmuka) behind [the food]. Therefore, he places the firebrand behind the food. [He offers] those who possess forms...
Releasing themselves and wearying, they move by their own inherent power (*svadhā*), turning away from the one who is behind and toward the one who is in front.
Agni drives him away from this world; for Agni is the dispeller of darkness. Therefore, he places it right there.
Then, a layering of *darbha* grasses, distinguished by having a single root and other such qualities, should be performed there.

"In that place, one should then [spread] many auspicious *darbha* grasses with a single root."
He drew up the water-vessels with their mouths facing south, reciting the mantras over them simultaneously.

"In that place" means where the morsels (*piṇḍas*) are to be offered. "From there" means immediately after the digging and so forth. "Darbhas" refers to *kuśa* grass; in its absence, the *kāśa* grass and others previously mentioned [should be used].

"One whose crest is joined to a single [other] rice-grain"—the word "śivān" (auspicious ones) refers to those characterized by such attributes as having tips that have not been split by *māyā*. Since the plural number itself establishes the completion [of the sense], the suffix "-ka" is used to indicate the constant nature [of the act]. And because no specific distinctions are mentioned, [the term applies] even to a single lump (*piṇḍa*).

From that point onward, there is no restriction regarding the number [of morsels] up to the covering [of the stomach], as one may proceed according to desire and possibility; for other [types of] food have a visible purpose. If it is argued that there is a restriction because another supporting substance (ādhāra) is understood to prevent the falling of the morsels, we say no; for even in the absence of a substance to prevent the falling of the morsels, [the practice remains].
Because the intervention of *dhā*, *bhūta*, and *bhṛ* is established by only a few instances of *darbha*; [therefore, there is no intervention] by all [of them].
In the section on the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*) in the *Prākalpa*, [it is stated]:

"The world does not exist for him at all. Those for whom he is to the south are called 'those to whom he is southward' (*dakṣiṇāyaḥ*). [He is] 'one whose feet are turned toward the north' (*udakapādī*)."

"Udaṅmunnāḥ" means they should extend upward. "'Smṛṇuyāt'" means he should spread them out. "'Mama'"—that is, by my being the center, by my being the front, or by my being the root. Regarding this, Jānuka says:
"Let there be for me *upamanna* darbha grass, not left-over and not placed down.
"*Upamanna*" means near the root; the sense is that they have been cut here after reaching the roots.

And likewise, regarding the nature of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa states: "That which is cut at the joint belongs to the gods; that which is between the joints belongs to human beings; that which is the root belongs to the ancestors. then,
having paid homage to the gods, one should cause the eastern portion to be offered.
"Previously" means before the ancestors. "Portion" refers to the food to be offered to them.

"When there is only one Brahmin and a second is not available..."
For the ancestors, one should employ a Brāhmaṇa; for the gods, however, one should employ Agni.
Regarding the method for the ritual of the *anaṅga* [offering] at this sacred seat (*pīṭha*), Bṛhaspati says: "If,
due to the scarcity of the materials for the śrāddha, one should feed only a single person, then having drawn out small portions from each of those [meals], one should present that food to them."

Having taken a portion from a collection of various kinds of food prepared by a single Brahmin ascetic, and having set aside six portions, he should serve one portion upon a single dish or in a single vessel and offer it one by one, beginning with the *piṇḍa*, to each of the deities of the *śrāddha*.
Or rather,
having extracted it little by little from this very collection of atoms, one should consume it as if it were a pill.

One should offer [the food] after having separately prepared it. A specific distinction must be made.
Vasiṣṭha states it as follows:
One should offer that food either into the fire or to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). As stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "Then one should offer the food into the fire or to a celibate student."
"Then," meaning having performed the ancestral rites (*pitrya*) up to the point of requesting permission to eat;
regarding this, Śātātapa describes the manner of satisfying many ancestors through a single Brāhmaṇa:
"A single Brāhmaṇa may indeed become the fivefold manifestation of the Śrāddha."
The three ancestors have been declared; how can those three go?
The fathers reside on the chest, the grandfathers on the left side,
the great-grandfathers on the right, and the descendants behind.

The term ‘anuyāyinaḥ’ refers to the *piṇḍa-pramṛtis* (those who partake of the funeral cakes). Regarding the word ‘anuyāyinaḥ’, there is an alternative reading, ‘piṇḍatarkakāḥ’; this should be explained as referring to the elder paternal great-grandfathers and others who are entitled to a portion of the *piṇḍa-lepa* (the smearings of the cake).
In the *Prabhāsacaṇḍa* and *Devalasmṛti*, it is stated:
"The father eats from the hand of the twice-born; the grandfather eats from the mouth;
the great-grandfather eats from the [same] body; and the maternal grandfather is likewise remembered."
The paternal great-grandfather is the heart, while the grandfather is situated at the navel.
‘Bṛddhaḥ’ means one whose paternal grandfather is deceased.
Regarding the non-availability of even a single Brāhmaṇa, another alternative method is stated in the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa:
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, Chapter 16.
O dear one, in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kausika Viṭ should be employed;
with a concentrated mind, one should thus perform the Śrāddha for the six deities.
He who causes a division [of the offerings] becomes a slayer of his ancestors.

"A *kauśa* [is] made of *kuśa* grass; a *vaṭu* is a small human effigy. Having imagined that [effigy] as a worthy Brahmin, one should perform the entire *śrāddha*. 'Vibhakti' means a division or a portion of the ritual action;
one should not omit that."
Devala states the procedure for the *śrāddha* among the students:
"Having placed blades of *darbha* grass upon the seats, being composed in mind,
he should carry out the ritual procedure including the primary and secondary injunctions."
"Among the *śramaṇas*": those who have been invited to sit as Brahmins. "Welcome to you; I shall perform the *śrāddha*;

please grant me the opportunity (*kṣaṇa*) for the *śrāddha*; I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors; I shall perform the *śmīkaraṇa*"—such questions are "directions" (*praiṣas*), and their responses are "counter-directions" (*anupraiṣas*); both of these together constitute [the category].

One should perform the *vidhāna*— the section concerning the procedure for the *śrāddha*— oneself. Furthermore, he himself has stated what must be done regarding the food that has been resolved upon for that purpose.
In the absence of a vessel, a person, having performed the ritual of the ancestral sacrifice using another's [vessel], [should proceed].
Even after pointing out the food, one should take it up and go to where the vessel is.
"In the absence of a vessel, one should give it to a Brahmin, a cow, or even in water;
for there is no omission of what has been obtained, especially that which pertains to the ancestors."
And in the absence of the primary substances, others are also [permissible] out of compassion;
these are called the *tamāma* śrāddhas.
This is stated here in the *Parāśara-smṛti*, the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, and the *Vārāha-purāṇa*.
One who is incapable of performing a meritorious deed (avadāna) is marked by his own measure of grain.
In the ritual manual for the offering of the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*),
one should also bestow a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the twice-born, even if it be only a copper coin.

The meaning of this is as follows: in the absence of cooked food, one should offer to the invited twice-born (dvijas) grains such as wheat, rice, and so forth—which serve as the raw materials suitable for *śrāddha*—having dedicated them to the Viśvedevas and the ancestors (*pitṛs*), whether they have been cooked or uncooked. Since those grains are inedible due to their measure [of size], they cannot be consumed as a meal.

In this context, there is an omission of the entire class of properties associated with that [grain]. By the word *āśa*—derived from the root *aś*, meaning "to eat"—this is recalled through the specific qualification of the grain: that having returned to its own place, those [grains] must be made fit for eating as *brahma-anna* (food of Brahman) and consumed, but must not be employed for any other purpose. Otherwise—
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence [of the ritual being] ineffective.
Vyāsa states the specific rule regarding its performer:
"Only gold that is new and intended for the *śrāddha* may be taken from a Kṣatriya or others."
A Brahmin himself may employ this [text] as he desires, provided it is endowed with prosperity.

Regarding the phrase "from the Kṣatriya and so forth," this refers to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Mūrdhāvasikta, and others. Although it is stated here in general terms that "it may be employed as one pleases," nevertheless, it should not be employed in rites such as the Śrāddha; for once something has been relinquished with reference to one deity, it is improper to relinquish it again with reference to another deity. Therefore...

It should be understood that in worldly activities such as eating, as well as in non-worldly ones prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, the right hand and so forth must always be employed for obligatory and occasional rites; it is not restricted [to the right hand] alone in this regard. Here, one should eat oneself as much as has been accepted.

It should not be thought that there is a restrictive rule [regarding the Śūdra]; rather, it must be determined that one should perform the appropriate reception for a *śrāddha* intended for the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*) up until the end of the *triḥ* [verse]. However, one may accept [gifts] from a Śūdra.

It is stated in the *Ṣaḍāśītisamaya* that [the food] should not be employed for any rite, whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), but should be used solely for one's own meal or the meal of another;
whatever daily fee (*śrāddhika*) is received from Śūdras constitutes labor.
*Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, Supplemental Section (*Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), page 566.
All of that is sufficient for food, both for daily meals and for occasional ones.
Regarding this, Vyāsa has stated the quantity of grain to be given and the procedure:
"O son of Kuntī, one should give the *śrāddha* food, and one should give four times as much cooked rice."
But whatever rule there may be regarding the state of torpor, that rule applies to the raw rice meal as well.
O Bhārata, all rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should be performed;

one should give [the food] to the twice-born, or even that which is most excellent, and with that very same [food] one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) and present the rice-balls (piṇḍas).
In the *Ṣaḍatriṃśanmata*, another alternative regarding the offering of the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is also stated:
"At that time, the knower of the rites should perform the *āma-śrāddha* according to the procedure for the *śrāddha*;
he should perform the taking of the hand of the Brāhmaṇa according to the injunction."

The meaning is that one should give four times as much grain as the amount of food required for the feeding of the Brahmins to each individual Brahmin. Regarding the alternative for one unable to give fourfold, he [the author] states the following:
"O son of Kuntī, give with vigor; that gift shall become twofold,
or even threefold or fourfold, but one should never offer it grudgingly."
By the phrase "beginning with invocation" (*śrāvāhanādau*), the offering of water for the feet (*arghya*) and so forth are included.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"The invocation must be performed by you, and likewise the offering of the *arghya*."
This very same rule applies wherever a śrāddha ceremony is performed.
From the *Kūrmapurāṇa* and *Yamapurāṇa*:
"A Brāhmaṇa who is beset by calamities may always subsist on meat;
with that [meat] he should perform the *anvāhāryaka* offering, and with that very same [meat] he should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*)."
[Page 567] 16. The Chapter on the Offering of Pindas (Piṇḍadāna-prakaraṇa) in the Śrāddhakalpa.
Regarding the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), there is also another alternative:
when one performs the Śrāma-śrāddha, how should the offering of the rice-ball be conducted?

Having emerged from his own house-cooking, one should, free from envy, offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) according to what is available— either with milk-rice (pāyasa) or with sesame seeds— using the remnants.
Even the scattering of offerings (vikira) and so forth must be performed with uncooked food alone.
Thus says Pracetas:
"The offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) and likewise the pouring of water (nīkaraṇa) should be done by one who gives the Śrāddha with uncooked food."
Whatever may be offered there as part of a śrāddha rite, he should give that very thing at that place.

The meaning is that whatever else there may be, such as scattered offerings (vikira) and so forth, that too must be performed by that very same person. At the vehicle, at the utterance of "svadhā," and at the dismissal, the mantras are to be recited.
Other [rites] may be performed at different times; this is the rule remembered for the *gama-śrāddha*.

In the invocation mantra (*śrāvāhana-mantra*), at the phrase *śratta vaḥ*, there is the modification (*ūha*) to *svīkarta vaḥ*. In the *svadhākāra* mantra, beginning with *namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*, the word *dṛṣat* is to be modified to *amadravyasya*. In the dismissal mantra (*visarjana*), at the phrase *vāje vāje*, the position of the word *tṛptāḥ* is to be filled by *tarpasvat*.
This is the meaning. However, even when cooked food is available, a Śūdra must perform a *śramaśrāddha*, as was stated previously;
the method for its performance is shown in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
If those who know the Dharma perform prostrations toward the Dharma,
the ritual of bowing and the mantra of homage are prescribed.
Listen to how the invocation and other rites should be performed for a Śūdra.

O hero, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and other oblations to the gods, the deities, and the ancestors by their names and lineages; likewise, one should do so according to their names and lineages.
*Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, Supplemental Section (*Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), page 568.

[16 a0] "Homage" (*namaskāraḥ*) refers to the word *namaḥ*. "Homage to Agni Kavyavāhana; homage to Soma Pitṛmat. The mention of the *anvāhārya* (funeral) rite is illustrative; this same mantra is used elsewhere as well.
And likewise, with reference to the Śūdra, it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa and other texts:
"One should not omit the five great sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
And this mantra is prescribed for the Śūdra as a rule that excludes all other mantras. Thus, for him...
The exclusion of other mantras is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"In this very same way, a Śrāddha must also be performed by a Śūdra;
for indeed, everything for a Śūdra is ordained to be without mantras."

"In this very manner" means precisely according to the procedure for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. Since the *gotra* of Śūdras does not exist here, the term "gotra" must refer to the case of a Śūdra born from a twice-born man (*dvijātīyaja*). Alternatively, [it may refer to the lineage of the progenitor].

Therefore, according to the Vedic revelation, "All creatures are descended from Kaśyapa," it follows that the *gotra* for all Śūdras must be Kāśyapa. For this very reason, Vyāghrapāda established the rule:
"In the absence of a *gotra*, however, [the *gotra* is] Kaśyapa."
Even in the absence of cooked rice (śrāma-anna), a golden śrāddha (hema-śrāddha) should be performed.
And so says Marīci:
"In the absence of even cooked rice, a wise man should perform the śrāddha."
It was indeed four times the amount of grain, consisting of highly lustrous gold.

The meaning is as follows: in a *śramaśrāddha*, one should give to each individual Brāhmaṇa four times as much grain as is given to a single Brāhmaṇa, and in a *hemaśrāddha*, one should give to each individual Brāhmaṇa as much gold as can be obtained for that same amount of wealth. Here, those who, by considering the relative degree of their capacity, [perform] the *śramaśrāddha* with the giving of grain...

The various types of the substratum (*guṇin*) and so forth have been explained; accordingly, the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabheda*) regarding the probans (*hetu*) is also understood through this very same [explanation] of the object.

Dharma, however, said:
"Gold is declared to be twice the weight of silver, and that [silver] is four times the weight of copper."
In the absence of a Śrauta fire, [one should offer] for the twice-born, and especially for the Brāhmaṇa.

The meaning is that for each individual Brāhmaṇa, there should be four times as much gold as the amount of grain required to satisfy him completely. By this, it is stated that twice as much gold as the double measure of grain should be given.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*,
Vyāsa says:
"In the absence of a sacred fire, in the absence of a twice-born [preceptor], while traveling abroad, or upon the birth of a son..."
Likewise, the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the act of gathering [disciples] are permitted even for women and Śūdras.
In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born priests, during travel abroad, upon the birth of a son,
or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform a Hema-śrāddha (a śrāddha with gold).
An exception to the golden *śrāddha* is mentioned in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In the absence of sacrificial food (*anna*), in the absence of twice-born Brahmins, during travel abroad, or upon the birth of a son,
one should perform the *śrāddha*, excluding only the day of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)."
In this regard, wherever the *nāma-śrāddha* (name-śrāddha) is prescribed in other Smṛtis and various Purāṇas, there [it is to be performed].

It must be explained that the *hemaśrāddha* (gold-śrāddha) is prescribed only when raw grains (*āmadravya*) are unavailable; in this way, there will be no dilemma regarding the fault of lacking raw materials. Since grain, being the primary constituent of food, is more intimately related to the performance of the *śrāddha*, its prior adoption is favored whenever it is available, as opposed to external items.

It occurs as follows: on the occasion of the birth of a son, even though there is the presence of *madya* (intoxicants) and *coranna* (food stolen by thieves), one should perform the *śrāddha* itself.
For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"Upon the birth of a son, a wise man should perform the *śrāddha*."
*Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, Section on Supplements (*Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), [Page 570]
[16.50] Neither with cooked nor with raw food should one seek after auspicious things.
The method for offering the *piṇḍas* is also shown here in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"Having taken [food] from the household cooking, one should perform the offering of *piṇḍas* with water,
milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or gold, when the *Śrāddha* has been performed."
A Śūdra, however, should offer those funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with food cooked in his own household;
it is recorded in the tradition that for him, these may consist of parched grain flour, roots, fruits, or milk-rice (pāyasa).
The phrase "for the purpose of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa)" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. According to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"There is no invitation (*āmantraṇa*), no offering into the fire (*anvāhārya*), and no sacrificial portions (*vikara*) are given."
Nor indeed should the mind be directed toward this by anyone at all.
Having stated that grain received at a *śrāddha* performed by a *śūdra* must not be employed for obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* says:
"However, gold received at such a *śrāddha* does not incur any fault."
Therefore, he should perform his daily rites; gold is not called food.

However, he who is unable to perform the Śrāddha— which involves many components such as the invocation (āvāhana) and the like, and which is joined with the extensive procedure beginning with the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa)— should perform the Mārkaṇḍeya Śrāddha. And so says Saṃvarta:
If one is able to perform my entire Pārvaṇa rite here on earth, even according to my own prescribed rule at the proper time, it is ordained for him.
The renunciation of food that is to be eaten from a vessel is called *sat* (the good);
the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) prompted by that [renunciation] is designated by that term,

One should not cause the Aratri lamp, the Manaukarana water, or the rice balls (piṇḍas) to be offered.

One must not fill the vessel to the brim with water and the like; the meaning is that no food (artha) should be offered. Furthermore, the invocation accompanied by mantras is prohibited, but not the mere act of invocation itself, because without that, there would be no presence of the deities, and thus the performance of the *śrāddha* would be impossible. "One should not scatter [the food]; one should cast the morsels directly into the mouth."

Chāgaleya states that even one who is incapable of performing the rites such as the invocation (*śrāvāhana*) and the offering of food into the fire (*anaukaraṇa*), should at times perform the *śrāddha* according to the prescribed rule alone:

At that time, O twice-born one, the vow must be performed with faith according to the rule.

Regarding the specific performer and the restriction [of the rite], Vyāsa states that the *saṅkalpa-śrāddha* is as follows: "One who has not performed the *pārvaṇa*, nor the *ekoddiṣṭa*, nor the *sapiṇḍana*,
should perform the *saṅkalpa* for the *piṇḍa-kriyā* and then feed [the Brahmins]."

Since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha is performed only for one whose fire has been extinguished (*atyantāgni*), therefore, for those who have abandoned their fires, only the *mahāśrāddha* should be performed; thus it is said in the *Triṃśanmata*.
O Brahmin, when one is without a wife or likewise when the sacred fires have been extinguished,

But one who possesses the *sānnayya* [should perform] the procedure for the *sānnayya*, or else the offering of flour mixed with jujube fruits (*badara*) and the like.

Now, if you have an exceedingly great need for the word "separately" (pṛthak), let not this statement regarding the flowering creeper cause you confusion; let it be so, O Sumanas, according to your mind.
Indeed—
At the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, one should feed the Brahmins just as at the Parvan rites;
however, for the sake of the deceased, the Ekoddiṣṭa should be performed separately according to the prescribed rule.
O Hero, O King, one should perform both the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa* śrāddhas at the *apiṇḍīkaraṇa*; thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva.

If that were so, the word *punaḥ* (again) would be appropriate. It is not so. From the word *punaḥ*, this meaning is understood: having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) for the ancestors, one should afterwards perform it for the deceased (*preta*). Not [otherwise].
And there is no such statement anywhere among those very Brāhmaṇas that a deceased person (preta) should be summoned [to the feast].
Now, if this were the case, it would result in favoring greatness; well then, let us favor greatness by feeding only one person for the sake of all! But this is not tenable, for nine—

"Vaikaṃ (one rice-ball) is declared for all [ancestors] in the piṇḍas," according to the statement of Śaunaka. Furthermore, as for the statement of Manu, "One should feed even a single person at both the rite for the gods and the rite for the ancestors," its scope must necessarily be restricted to the *saṃpiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony; for that which is offered to only one [deity] is designated as *ekoddiṣṭa*, whereas [the *saṃpiṇḍīkaraṇa*] is performed for three.
Where it is offered, there it is the *pārvaṇa* rite. However, when the *pārvana* and the *ekoddiṣṭa* are performed simultaneously at one and the same time, then that is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

This is because, in the case of a single [deceased], there is necessarily no separate performance of the *ekoddiṣṭa*; therefore, just as there is a distinction of Brahmins [in the *pārvaṇa*], so too [is there a distinction here].
Alternatively, the connection with the *pārvaṇa* rite must be stated in this way:

even when the deceased is a Brahmin such as a paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*), there should be the favor of the rule "an odd number for the ancestors" (*pitrya ayugmān*). However, that [favor] does not apply here because these two—the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*—are distinct.

If, however, one who has been dead for a long time is designated by the word *preta*, then there is no fault whatsoever, because for such a person there is an absence of the offering of water and *arghya*. The word "first" (*ādya*) here also refers to the human body (*puruṣapiṇḍa*). If one asks how this is so, it is according to the statements of the *Kāṭhaka* and *Gṛhya* texts. Furthermore, the use of the word "first" is not tenable if it were intended to mean the non-existence of the deceased body. Alternatively, the term "deceased" (*preta*) may refer to one who has died recently.

Then this [text] would be appropriate: "He who offers a separate piṇḍa to a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed incurs sin and suffers affliction. For for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not yet occurred, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed every year; however, when [the deceased] has long been remembered [as having attained union], [the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs].

Regarding that which is designated by the term *preta* (the deceased), since there is no separate offering for it until the *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, this prohibition is appropriately understood [to apply]. Therefore, the claim that "in the rites for the paternal great-grandfather and others, the merging of the *piṇḍa* into the *piṇḍas* must be performed" is indeed incorrect; for if that were the case, then in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*... [the great-grandfather]... would be [rendered redundant].

Since the two highly precious *piṇḍas* would be subjected to contact with other *piṇḍas* even in this [present] life, it would logically follow that they themselves undergo the *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. However, this does not apply to a deceased person who has already undergone the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. It is more appropriate that the merging of the two *piṇḍas* into the others should be performed only for one who has recently died, whether long ago or just now. For this reason, it is so.

It might be argued that the offering of *arghya* for one who has recently died would not be possible [if the water were already used]. To this we reply: the offering of that *arghya* is accomplished by means of the water remaining in the vessel of the ancestors (*pitṛ-pātra*). For there is no scriptural statement to the effect that the remainder must be discarded. Furthermore, as for the etymological derivation of "preta" from the sense of "one who has departed far away" (*prakṛṣṭa-praṇata*), [it does not preclude the use of the water].

It has been stated that the term *prata* refers to the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*); however, that too is clearly without due consideration, since Yājñavalkya, having established in the section on impurity (*āśauca*) that "food should be given for three days to those who know the ritual procedure," has now further stated: "one should offer food into the *pratapātra*."
At this very moment, because it is a great reality, it revolves within the intellect as something entirely new.

In the *śrāddha* for the gods (*deva-śrāddha*), the three deities are the celestial sages (*devarṣis*), the Brahman-sages (*brahmarṣis*), and the Vedic sages (*vaikhanasa-ṛṣis*). In the *śrāddha* for the quarters (*dika-śrāddha*), the three deities are the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. In the *śrāddha* for humans (*manuṣya-śrāddha*), the three deities are Manaka, Manandana, and Manātana.
In the *śrāddha* for beings (*bhūta-śrāddha*), the three deities are the elements beginning with earth (*pṛthivy-ādīni bhūtāni*) and the sense organs beginning with sight (*cakṣur-ādīni karaṇāni*).

The assembly of beings is fourfold. For the *piṇḍa-śrāddha*, there are three deities: the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; and the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather. For the *mātṛ-śrāddha*, there are three deities: the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. For the *ātma-śrāddha* (the rite for oneself), there are three deities.
[The ancestors are] one's self, father, and grandfather.

And one should feed a thousand Brāhmaṇas with great honor, along with appropriate sacrificial fees.
Or even a single person devoted to yoga, established in Brahman, with senses conquered—
by him alone one may indeed attain the great state of Rudra.
This entire specific procedure enjoined for the Śrāddha has been declared;
one should perform it after [the teacher] has died, or not at all, since he himself is already liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Or, he may perform the obligatory and occasional rites and so forth, or he may abandon them entirely.
Even upon his death, no impurity (āśauca) exists for him;
there is no doubt that he is purified by mere bathing alone.
If Vāma occurs in the *mūrti* of Pāta and Kumāra within one's own field (*svakṣetra*), then everything should be performed for him; even his son is a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*).
If the daughter of that great-souled one later became his mother— whether she was of the same caste or of another, and whether she was of good vows or not— [he would still honor her].
There is no doubt that even his own kinsmen are liberated;
there is no doubt here that the ancestors are released even from hell,
and likewise the parents are freed from all [karmic] bonds.
On the day of death, one may dig up the ground or burn it;
or, having performed the remaining duties for a son, no fault is found.
And by means of his subsequent karma, the Great-Souled One attained the higher states of existence;
all of this was related by Brahmā to the sages of purified soul.
Formerly, it was heard from Manatkumāra himself, by command and through his grace.

25th Chapter:
The Method for the Application of Jīvas in the Ritual Manual (Kalpa).
All this has been told to you out of compassion by that wise one.
It was told to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself by Brahmā,
due to the negligence of that illustrious god Vedavyāsa.
"I have understood it and indeed performed it solely by his command.
All this secret counsel has been told to you.
It must not be given to the wicked, nor should it be given to one who is not a disciple."
The commentary on this *Liṅgapurāṇa* will now be stated; thus [the author] has responded to the objection.

Regarding "on the path of the *śrāddha*," it refers to the section concerning the *śrāddha* and other rites; "sequence" (*krama*) means the specific form consisting of place, time, and so forth; "at the time of death" (*mṛtyukāle*) means at the moment of dying while reciting my mantra; and "in the eye of life" (*jīvanetre*) means by way of the aperture of the *brahmarandhra*.

The meaning is that one is indeed liberated through the attainment of the stainless knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Regarding the term "immortal" (*amṛta*), in the middle, having measured out from the opening (*vilāt*) toward the east and so forth, a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be prepared by the *Syaṇḍina* for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*).
Having worshipped Brahmā and the others with these mantras of Brahmā and the rest which are about to be described, one should [proceed] with those very [mantras].

One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks and so forth; having extracted each of the principles (tattvas) pertaining to the self— the elements that constitute the self— and having meditated upon them as if they were being clearly manifested one by one, [one should proceed].
Then, one should offer oblations (juhuyāt) directed toward the respective deity; thereafter, that [oblation] becomes pure and shines intensely.

In worship, the mantra ends with "namaḥ" (salutation), while in the fire sacrifice (homa), it ends with "svāhā. In that regard, for the beloved ones beginning with Brahmā, there is the offering (prajā-hāmi) to those respective deities, extending from the very first up to Paśupati.
Thus,

for the sake of illustration, he cites the first mantra from among the twenty-four mantras of the *Kāraṇāgama* and other tantras, beginning with "Śivāya matyam," etc., as the primary example. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
(1) He instructs [the sacrificer] by reciting the middle *ṣṭhalā* formula.
In the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, [Chapter 25, Section 6]:

"In due order, according to the previously mentioned method, the deities beginning with Viriñci and ending with Śiva [are to be worshipped] in the single-mantra rites; furthermore, [they are worshipped] in the order of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*)."

Having worshipped [the deities] in order, beginning with "To Agni, to Śiva, to Mṛtyu, Svāhā! and ending with "To Brahmā, Svāhā!", as well as Paśupati, his wife, and so forth, one should offer oblations individually, following the sequence of ghee, *caru*, and meat. Therein, "Oṃ Satya... and so on is the mantra for the oblation of pure clarified butter (*kevalājya-homa*), and the phrase "sarvaṃ dhag" is the [concluding] statement.
The third [mantra] is "bhuvah svāhā," and the fourth mantra is "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā.
Thus, one should offer these four mantras separately for Śiva and his consort.
Likewise, in this context, [the mantras are]: "jalaṃ me chindhi," "jihvāyāṃ gmaṃ," "bhava me'ghaṃ jahi," and "bhūḥ svāhā."

The oblation (*homa*) is performed with the four mantras beginning with *tyādi* as modified [for each ancestor], as well as with the *viraja* mantras, and with the six mantras beginning with *prāṇe niviṣṭa*. The Śrāddha offering is made according to the rules of one's own domestic ritual (*svagṛhya*), and the oblation is likewise offered for the father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth. Having thus performed the oblation every day for seven days, on the seventh day, having eaten...
Having worshipped the Brahmins according to the instruction of the heart-deity, eight *piṇḍas* should be offered to all [the ancestors] beginning with the father.

When the *auva* (ancestral) śrāddha has been performed in this manner, there is no impurity (*āśauca*) nor the state of death (*mṛtaka*) if one's own kinsman dies. Likewise, a son born from him should also be consecrated with the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and other sacraments of his father and others, and he shall become a knower [of the truth].
The same applies to a daughter. Furthermore, these two are born through the practice of yoga by the practitioner.
Thus ends the *Pariśeṣa* [section] of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, Śrī Mahādevīya, the sovereign of all administrative departments, the Paṇḍita Śrī Hemādri.
The section on the ritual procedure for the *jauvacchrāddha* (śrāddha performed while the donor is still alive) within the *Khaṇḍa-Śrāddhakalpa* is completed.

In the Bhayapurāṇa,
there is a description of the nature of the Śrāddha.
O protector of the earth, this much has been told to you, the faithful one; it is that which was taught by the Sage,
which removes evil and increases merit.
In the world, however, its primacy is exactly so.

May the dense mass of my merit, which has begun its descent upon the limbs of the Lord of the Earth, somehow attain even a slight touch of his feet, the mere mention of whose name is not easily obtained by anyone.
Therefore, this great work, the *Śrāddhanibandhana*, composed by the illustrious Karaṇa Ve Hamādri, shall steal away the wealth of those who hold [other] opinions.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha*.
